title: Alternating Characters
directAnswer: You never need to decide which character to delete — you only need to count how many adjacent pairs are equal. Walk the string once and count every position i where s[i] == s[i-1]. That count is the minimum number of deletions, because each equal-neighbour collision forces exactly one removal. O(n) time, O(1) space.

rules: The answer is **exactly** the number of indices `i` where `s[i] == s[i-1]` — no more, no less.
You don't choose *which* duplicate to delete; in a run of `k` equal characters you must delete `k − 1`, and counting collisions counts those automatically.
Compare each character to its **left neighbour**, never to a fixed previous-kept variable you forgot to update.
A single character or an already-alternating string yields `0` — the loop simply never fires.
This is greedy and optimal in one pass; there is no need to rebuild the string.
whenToUse: You must make a string 'alternating' or 'no two adjacent equal' with minimum edits
Deletions only (not replacements) and the cost is uniform per deletion
The decision at each position depends only on the immediate neighbour
You can count collisions instead of simulating the removals
antiSignals: Replacements or insertions are allowed too → it becomes an edit-distance / DP problem
You must output the resulting string, not just the count → still O(n) but you build output
'Alternating' means a strict A/B/A/B alphabet, not merely 'no two adjacent equal' → different rule
Costs differ per character → greedy collision count no longer equals the optimum
remember.takeaway: When deletions are uniform and the constraint is purely local ('no two adjacent equal'), the minimum number of deletions equals the number of adjacent equal pairs. Counting collisions beats simulating removals — the same idea powers 'remove adjacent duplicates' and run-length compression problems.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you realise you don't have to simulate deletions at all — that the answer is a pure count of adjacent equal pairs, derivable from a single left-to-right scan.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Building a new string by skipping duplicates and then computing the difference in lengths — correct but more work and more bug surface than just counting collisions.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Argue why counting is optimal: in any maximal run of k identical characters you are forced to delete exactly k − 1, and the run contributes exactly k − 1 collisions. Sum over runs = total collisions.

problemStatement:
You are given a string `s` containing only the characters `A` and `B`. A string is **alternating** if no two adjacent characters are the same (e.g. `ABAB`, `BABA`).

In one operation you may delete any single character. Return the **minimum number of deletions** required to turn `s` into an alternating string.
constraints: s consists only of the characters 'A' and 'B'
Only deletions are allowed (no insertions or replacements)
understanding: Wherever two equal characters sit next to each other, one of them has to go. A run of identical characters of length k (say AAAA) must collapse to a single character, costing k − 1 deletions. You are not asked for the resulting string — only the count — so you can sum those forced deletions directly by counting adjacent equal pairs.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the alphabet contain only A and B?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, by the prompt. But the counting solution doesn't depend on that — it works for any alphabet, since the rule is purely 'no two adjacent equal'.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I use insertions or replacements?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No, deletions only. If replacements were allowed the answer would still be the same here, but framing it as deletions keeps the greedy count exact.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I return the count or the final string?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The count of deletions. That's why we can avoid building any output and just tally collisions.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What about an empty or single-character string?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Already alternating — zero deletions. The loop starts at index 1, so length-0 or length-1 inputs return 0 naturally.

approaches.name: Rebuild the Alternating String (Naive)
approaches.whenToMention: Mention to show you understand the mechanics, then point out it does extra work versus pure counting.
hints: Imagine literally producing the alternating string: scan left to right and keep a character only if it differs from the last one you kept.
Append each kept character to a builder. The number of deletions is then |s| minus the length of what you kept.
This is correct, but you're allocating an output buffer just to subtract two lengths — can you skip building it?
approaches.complexityReasoning: One pass to build the filtered string is O(n) time, but the StringBuilder / list holding the survivors costs O(n) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
The literal reading is: construct the alternating result, then report how many characters you dropped. Walk the string, track the last character you decided to keep, and append the current character only when it differs.

**Why it is correct.** Keeping a character only when it differs from the previous *kept* one is exactly the greedy rule that produces a maximal alternating subsequence. Two equal neighbours can never both survive, so every survivor differs from its predecessor — the result is alternating by construction.

**Why the deletion count falls out.** Every input character is either kept or dropped. If `kept` characters survive, then `|s| − kept` were deleted. Subtracting the two lengths gives the answer.

**Why we don't ship it.** It is correct but wasteful: you allocate an `O(n)` buffer purely to throw it away after measuring its length. The problem only wants the *count*, and the count is fully determined by how many times two equal characters touch — which you can tally without storing anything. Use this version to explain the mechanics, then collapse it into the counting solution.
approaches.insight: Building the survivors and then doing |s| − kept is the same arithmetic as counting collisions: every dropped character corresponds to exactly one collision with the character kept before it.

dryRun.intro: Keep a character only if it differs from the last kept one; deletions = |s| − kept.

java.explanation: Keep c only when the buffer is empty or its last character differs — this enforces alternation.
Everything not kept was deleted, so the difference is the deletion count.

python.line: if not kept or kept[-1] != c:
python.explanation: Append c only if it differs from the last survivor (or nothing is kept yet).

pitfalls: Allocating an O(n) buffer when only a counter is needed.
Comparing against the previous INPUT character instead of the previous KEPT character — they coincide here, but the framing invites bugs.
Forgetting the empty-buffer guard before reading the last kept character.

approaches.name: Count Adjacent Equal Pairs (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The intended answer. Phrase it as 'the minimum deletions equals the number of adjacent equal pairs'.
hints: You don't need the resulting string — only its size relative to the input. What single quantity captures every forced deletion?
A character must be deleted precisely when it equals the character immediately before it. Count those positions.
Loop i from 1 to n−1; whenever s[i] == s[i−1], increment a counter. Return the counter. No extra memory.
approaches.complexityReasoning: A single left-to-right scan touching each character once is O(n) time. Only an integer counter is stored → O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
Walk the string from index 1 and increment a counter every time the current character equals the one before it. That counter is the answer.

**Why a collision forces exactly one deletion.** Consider a maximal *run* of identical characters — say `AAAA`. To make it valid, only one of those `A`s may remain, so you must delete `k − 1` of them for a run of length `k`. Now count the adjacent equal pairs inside that run: positions `(0,1), (1,2), (2,3)` — exactly `k − 1` of them. Run length minus one equals the number of internal collisions. So counting collisions counts forced deletions, run by run.

**Why summing over the whole string is still exact.** Distinct runs are separated by a character change, and a character change is *not* a collision, so runs never share or double-count pairs. Adding up `(k − 1)` across every run is the same as adding `1` for every adjacent equal pair anywhere in the string. The grand total is the minimum number of deletions.

**Why this is optimal, not just correct.** You can never do better than `k − 1` deletions in a run of `k` equal characters — fewer would leave two equal neighbours somewhere. And you never need more, because deleting down to one survivor per run already makes the string alternating. So the collision count is simultaneously a lower bound and an achievable upper bound — it *is* the optimum.

**Why no extra space.** You never store the result string; you only compare each character with its predecessor and bump an integer. That's `O(1)` auxiliary space regardless of input size.
approaches.insight: Reframing 'minimum deletions' as 'count of local collisions' removes the entire question of *which* character to delete. Whenever the cost is uniform and the constraint is purely between neighbours, counting violations is the optimum — you never simulate the fix.

dryRun.intro: Compare each character with its left neighbour; tally equalities. No string is built.

java.explanation: Start at 1 so s[i-1] is always valid; length-0/1 strings skip the loop entirely → 0.
An equal left neighbour is a forced deletion — the heart of the algorithm.
Each collision contributes exactly one removal; no decision about which side to drop is needed.

python.explanation: Begin at index 1 so s[i-1] exists; tiny strings return 0 with no iterations.
Adjacent equality means one of the two must go.
Tally the forced deletion directly — no resulting string is constructed.

diagrams.title: Scanning for adjacent collisions
diagrams.caption: Highlighted cells mark a position equal to its left neighbour — each is one deletion.

edgeCases.behavior: Loop never runs (no index 1) → returns 0. Single characters are already alternating.
Four collisions → 4 deletions, collapsing a run of 5 to a single A.

pitfalls: Off-by-one: starting the loop at 0 and reading s[i-1] = s[-1] (Python wraps to the last char; Java throws).
Trying to decide which character to delete — unnecessary; the count alone is the answer.
Assuming the alphabet matters; the collision count works for any characters.

commonMistakes: Simulating deletions by repeatedly scanning and removing until stable — O(n²) for no benefit over a single-pass count.
Comparing each character to the first character or a stale 'previous' variable instead of the immediate left neighbour.
Off-by-one errors reading s[i-1] when i starts at 0.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Repeated-scan removal until stable
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Removing one character per collision and rescanning the whole string each time is O(n²). A single pass already counts every forced deletion.
commonMistakesDetailed.good: return sum(1 for i in range(1, len(s)) if s[i] == s[i-1])

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Comparing to a stale 'previous' value
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If you cache prev but forget to update it on a non-deletion, you compare against the wrong character and miscount.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Off-by-one on the left neighbour
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Starting at i = 0 and reading s[i-1] reads index -1; in Python that silently wraps to the last character and corrupts the count.

patternNote: Local-constraint collision counting. When deletions are uniform and the only rule is 'no two adjacent equal', the minimum number of deletions equals the number of adjacent equal pairs — count violations in one pass instead of simulating fixes. The same run-length insight underlies adjacent-duplicate removal and string compression.
